subject: electronics
title: Sensor divider: darkness switches the lamp on

segments.say: Bright daylight: the circuit assembles, lamp off. A 6 V supply drives a fixed resistor and an LDR in series, and the output is taken across the LDR. In bright daylight the LDR resistance is low, so it takes only a small share of the supply and the lamp stays off. Point at the 1.2 V voltmeter reading on your student notes diagram before the light changes.
questions: What is the LDR resistance in bright daylight, and what share of the supply does it take?
Why does a low resistance take only a small share of the 6 V supply?

segments.say: Light falls: resistance steps up, output climbs. The LDR resistance steps up to 1 kOhm, equal to the fixed resistor, so the supply splits evenly and the output climbs to 3.0 V - still below the threshold. Now try the divider questions on your worksheet.
questions: Why does the output reach exactly 3.0 V at this stage?
Is 3.0 V enough to switch the lamp on, and how do you know?

segments.say: Dusk: the output stops just below the threshold. The LDR resistance steps up to 2.3 kOhm and its share climbs to 4.2 V - close to, but still just below, the 4.5 V threshold, so the lamp stays off. Check the dusk reading against your student notes before moving on.
questions: How close is the dusk output to the threshold, and why is close not enough?
What must happen to the LDR resistance for the output to cross 4.5 V?

segments.say: Dark: the output crosses the threshold and the lamp lights. The LDR resistance rises to 9 kOhm, so it takes 5.4 V of the 6 V supply and switches the lamp on. Keep the rising-share order as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
questions: Why does the biggest resistance take the biggest share of the supply?
At which earlier stages was the lamp off, and what single number decides it?
segments.watchFor: As it gets darker and the LDR's resistance rises, the voltage across the LDR falls, so the sensor output switches the lamp off. Listen for students who imagine a bigger resistance blocking voltage. Send them back to scene 4 and the 5.4 V voltmeter reading: In a series divider each resistor takes a share of the supply in proportion to its resistance, so as the LDR's resistance rises in the dark its share - the output voltage - climbs until it crosses the threshold and switches the lamp on.
